title: The Word as Revelation: Names of Gods
byline: by Ram Swarup · first published 1980 · Voice of India reprint 2001 · foreword by David Frawley
lede: Are words just labels, or do they express something of what they name? Ram Swarup starts from Plato's Cratylus and goes on to speech-sounds, how new things get named, roots and synonyms. His argument is that a word's meaning rises in layers, from the physical to the sensory, the mental and the intellectual, depending on which faculty of mind is using it and how pure that faculty is. At the top, he says, words become names of the soul's own powers, which is what the Vedic gods are. He rejects the reading of them as primitive nature-worship and ends with meditation on the divine names.

note: This is a work of religious philosophy rather than academic linguistics; its theory of sound and meaning is the author's own and speculative by his own admission (chapter 4). This page summarises it, attributed to him.

sections.title: Four approaches to the question
items: Socrates' idea in the Cratylus, and Hindu seers' idea of subtle sound: sounds carry psychic qualities.
Car, telephone, astronaut: new things get old words rather than invented ones.
Words have histories, and their meaning develops from a root.
One object suggests many ideas, so it gets many names; “dog” is his example.

sections.title: Two readings of the Vedic gods

items: Lacking a ranked hierarchy, so disordered
Every god has many names, as Agni does (ch. 10)
Neither one nor many: ekam sat, One Reality, differently named (ch. 11)

sections.title: The Names of Gods
items: Vishnu, Shiva, Ganesha, Rama, Krishna, the Mother: each has a thousand names.
In the Yoga of Devotion, names like Aum, Rama, Krishna and Shiva contain all levels of existence.
Their truths lie beyond ordinary desire-consciousness, so they speak only to a purified mind.
The names are for meditation, to take on something of their meanings and powers.
